newsitem.title: USA: Justice official says phone transition takes time.
newsitem.headline: Justice official says phone transition takes time.

text.p: Acting Assistant Attorney Joel Klein brushed aside complaints that consumers have been slow to see benefits of the new telecommunications law, saying Tuesday he was optimistic people will see the benefits of it.

"I've seen some recent stories in the press complaining that consumers haven't yet received the benefits of the 1996 (telecommunications) act, but frankly I think such expectations are unrealistic," he told a Glasser Legalworks Seminar on competitive policy in communications.

Klein said that after a century of a regulated telephone system, "it won't be deregulated in a year and even after it is deregulated, it'll take time for competition to wring all the fat out of the system."
But he said that eventually consumers will "truly get the best service at the lowest prices."
Klein said the government faces the paradox of choosing the form of intervention most likely to foster a free market in the future.

"We obviously think competition is the preferred alternative but it's very important that you get competition right in the transition," he told reporters after his speech. "Short-term gains that aren't lasting are really not a good solution."

Klein said that he believes the government must lay out one set of rules that allows long distance and other companies to provide local telephone service and another set of rules that permits long distance and other companies to provide local service.
He said the government should also cut back fees charged long distance companies to connect to local carriers.
He said the government must also find a new way to pay the costs of providing telephone service to low-income families.
